metadata.title: The World Is Falling - Extending Walker Jumpman
metadata.note: Walker-mode Godot walkthrough. B00 is a labelled reconstruction, never a transcript. All gameplay is native 3840x2160 captured from the running game; see CAPTURE.md. Claims are indexed in FACTCHECK.md.

beats.label: The ask
beats.narration_text: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a world where gravity has failed, where debris falls upward instead of down, and where the player finds an object that lets them fall upward too, into a playable Godot project. The chapter should run on one rule: the world shows you what you expect, not what is actually there. Some floors exist but are never drawn. Some are drawn but are not there. The player checks by turning gravity upside down.
beats.reconstruction_label: Illustrative reconstruction of the design ask - not a historical transcript.

beats.label: What was built
beats.narration_text: This is walker-jumpman, the course starter by Nik Bear Brown. The original is one short level: a few gaps, a spike, a finish flag, and a character drawn as four stacked rectangles. What you are about to see is that project extended. The character is now the Runner, whose trail length is its speed. The level is about five times longer and ends in a tower you cannot enter the normal way up. One chapter is built. Four more are written down in the design document and are not built, and I will not pretend otherwise.

artifactLines: four stacked rectangles, one short level
CHARACTER  the Runner - trail length is horizontal speed
LEVEL  960 -> 4980 px, finish moved into a tower shaft
SCOPE  one chapter built; four designed and NOT built

qc.sparse_reason: A reference card read aloud, not a busy graphic. Six short lines on a dark plate is the point - the viewer is meant to read them while Liam speaks, and filling the safe area with decoration would make them harder to read, not easier.

beats.label: The world falls up
beats.narration_text: This is the starter, extended. Debris falls upward. A sign says run right, reach the tower. The controls are unchanged, and the Runner's trail is its own speed.

shot.note: Native 3840x2160 capture from the running game; see CAPTURE.md.

qc.contrast_reason:
Gameplay plate, not a card, and two heuristics mis-fire on it.
full_bleed: the game renders edge to edge at 3840x2160. The world IS the frame, so crossing title-safe is the composition rather than overflow, and the HUD stays inside its own reserved bands.
contrast_regions: the whole-frame average is low because the upright palette is deliberately pale - light is the comfortable lie and dark is the truth, which is this chapter's mechanic rather than a rendering fault. The essential text is the PERSISTENT HUD, measured where hud.gd draws it: title, chapter and log count, controls row, and deaths/timer. Each must pass on its own.
The feather readout is deliberately NOT declared. It only exists after the player picks the feather up, so before that the region is legitimately empty - an earlier revision declared it and the gate correctly reported nine empty-region defects. Declaring a conditional element as persistent text would have been a false claim about the frame.

beats.label: Signs that lie
beats.narration_text: Now it lies in both directions. A drawn platform that holds nothing. A locked door that is not solid. Spikes that cannot hurt you, and under a sign reading safe, spikes that are never drawn at all.

beats.label: Why a floor can be invisible
beats.narration_text: Here is the source change behind all of that. The starter already walked its level data twice - once in ready, to build a collider for every solid, and once in draw, to paint them. Those two loops were always separate. Hidden geometry now joins only the first loop, so it collides without ever being painted. Phantom geometry joins neither, so it is painted and holds nothing. No new node types, no physics change, and not one collision check removed. The mechanic is the difference between two loops that already existed.

props.artifactTitle: Why a floor can be invisible
artifactLines: The starter already walked its level data twice:
_ready()  builds a collider for every solid
hidden  joins only the build loop  -> collides, never painted
phantom joins neither              -> painted, holds nothing
No new node types. No collision check removed.

beats.narration_text: The finish sits above the floor. A normal jump cannot reach it; only falling upward gets in. Then Enter replays it.

beats.label: Verdict
beats.narration_text: What is demonstrably working: the character reads correctly facing both ways, standing, jumping and inverted, against a collider that was never changed. Twenty-two landings past the original section. A relocated finish that the mechanic is required to reach. Seventy mechanics checks and nine keyboard checks passing, including all twenty-five the starter shipped with, none of them weakened. What is not settled: whether the Betrayal reads as fair or as cheap, and whether the environmental clues are legible at speed. The human playtest found three comprehension defects that every automated check had passed straight over - including a chapter that depended on a key it never taught the player. And one honest limitation: the light palette was the third attempt at the debris alone, and the design of those environmental clues is still being argued about.

props.artifactTitle: The World Is Falling - Extending Walker Jumpman
artifactLines: WORKS - 22 landings, relocated finish, 70 + 9 checks, 0 failures
WORKS - collider and tuning.gd byte-identical to the starter
UNSETTLED - is the Betrayal fair, or cheap?
UNSETTLED - are the environmental clues readable at speed?
LIMIT - 3 rows of the human playtest remain unverified
LIMIT - Chapters Two to Five are design text only

qc.sparse_reason: The verdict is six short lines that separate what works from what is unsettled. They are read aloud and meant to be read along with; padding the safe area with decoration would compete with the only thing on the card that matters.

beats.label: Your turn
beats.narration_text: Here is the experiment worth running. Take the starter, and before you add anything, find the two places it walks its level data - the loop that builds colliders and the loop that draws. Then add one array that joins only the first. You will have a floor a player can stand on and cannot see, in about twenty lines, and every existing test will still pass. Ask Walker for that, then go and find out whether your players read it as clever or as a trick. That answer is not in the code.
